golden-age-comics.context_blurb:
American comics begin on one cover, Action Comics #1 of 1938: the Krypton orphan raised on a farm is Superman. A graded copy sold in April 2024 for $6 million. Joe Shuster and Jerry Siegel had sold him for $130; the publicity around the 1978 Donner film finally won them stipends and credit.

Detective Comics #27, 1939: the Gotham heir orphaned in an alley is Bruce Wayne, and he is Batman. Bob Kane signed it, but the cape, cowl, name and Commissioner Gordon came from Bill Finger, credited at last in 2015.

Captain America #1, March 1941: Simon and Kirby's cover shows Steve Rogers punching Adolf Hitler. Fantastic Four #1 in 1961 was made by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. Lee signed off Excelsior, Latin for ever upward. Fellow artists called Kirby the King. The spider-bitten schoolboy from Queens is Peter Parker. Uncle Ben's lesson, first printed as the closing caption of his story and only later put in his mouth: with great power comes great responsibility. Thor's star-forged hammer, liftable only by the worthy, is Mjolnir. Lee and Steve Ditko's other great creation, a surgeon turned Sorcerer Supreme, is Doctor Strange. Daredevil's day job is lawyer in Hell's Kitchen. Comics' first major black superhero is Wakanda's king T'Challa, the Black Panther.

The bald Westchester telepath who schools young mutants is Professor Charles Xavier. The visored leader of the first five X-Men is Cyclops, Scott Summers. Wolverine, born James Howlett, carries adamantium grafted to every bone. Claremont and Byrne's 1980 story of Jean Grey as a world-eating firebird is the Dark Phoenix Saga.

Showcase #4 restarted the Flash as Barry Allen, a police forensic scientist. Hal Jordan's ring enrols him in the Green Lantern Corps. The grey monster who killed Superman in 1992 is Doomsday. Kirby's Fourth World set Darkseid's Apokolips against the paradise New Genesis.

Marvel's 1984 crossover on Battleworld was Secret Wars. Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen keeps returning to a yellow smiley badge with blood across one eye. Rorschach began as Moore's version of a Charlton hero DC withheld, the Question. Its mirrored fifth issue borrows its title from Blake's The Tyger. Miller's 1986 four-parter about an ageing Bruce Wayne is Batman: The Dark Knight Returns. His wife Lynn Varley coloured both that book and 300. Miller's Daredevil introduced the assassin Elektra Natchios. In Born Again the nun who nurses Matt back to health is Sister Maggie. Sin City opens on a scarred ex-convict hunting Goldie's killer, Marv. His 300 gave the internet a king kicking a messenger down a well: this is Sparta.

Mignola's red-skinned demon, summoned by Nazi occultists and raised by an American professor, is Hellboy. His true name is Anung Un Rama. Ennis's Preacher travels with Tulip and an Irish vampire, Cassidy. His Hitman is the mind-reading gun-for-hire Tommy Monaghan. His Punisher is Frank Castle, whose wife and children were gunned down in Central Park after they stumbled onto a mob killing. Bane, pumped full of the steroid Venom, breaks Batman's back in 1993. The Clone Saga brought Ben Reilly home to New York after years on the road, and there he became the Scarlet Spider. Brubaker's frozen Soviet assassin Bucky Barnes is the Winter Soldier. Bendis's 2011 replacement Spider-Man is Miles Morales. Kick-Ass made an eleven-year-old actress famous as Hit-Girl, Mindy Macready. Kingdom Come walks Pastor Norman McCay through his visions beside the Spectre.

Gaiman's Sandman follows Dream, whose cheerful elder sister with the ankh is Death. Its nineteenth issue, Shakespeare playing to the fairies, took the 1991 World Fantasy Award for Short Fiction. Smith's self-published Bone follows Fone, Smiley and the schemer Phoney Bone. Foster's Arthurian Sunday strip, running since 1937, is Prince Valiant. Hergé's fox terrier Milou became Snowy in English. Bloom County put its mangy parody of Garfield, Bill the Cat, on shirts and plush toys. Watterson refused to license Calvin and Hobbes for merchandise at all, so no plush Hobbes exists. Wonder Woman's creator, the psychologist William Moulton Marston, had already built an early prototype of the polygraph, the lie detector.

mcu-through-endgame.context_blurb:
Kevin Feige's Marvel Studios told one story across twenty-three films from 2008 to 2019, now called the Infinity Saga. It opens in an Afghan cave, where a kidnapped arms dealer welds an escape suit from his own missiles.

Jon Favreau directed it and gambled on an actor fresh out of drug arrests, Robert Downey Jr. The hero is Iron Man, the billionaire inventor Tony Stark. AC/DC's Back in Black plays over the opening convoy. Jeff Bridges, the partner selling Stark guns to terrorists, builds a huge grey copy of the cave suit: the Iron Monger. After the credits a one-eyed man named Nick Fury offers Stark a place in the Avengers Initiative.

Origins follow. The scrawny Brooklyn volunteer turned super-soldier, Steve Rogers, is played by Chris Evans. The German scientist who hands him the serum, shot by a Hydra spy minutes later, is Abraham Erskine. The hammer-carrying Asgardian out of Norse myth is Thor. His horned adopted brother, played by Tom Hiddleston, is Loki. The gamma-dosed scientist who goes green in a temper is Bruce Banner.

Joss Whedon put them in one film in 2012. Loki tears a hole in the New York sky with the cube called the Tesseract, and the blue scepter in his hand hides the Mind Stone. In Stuttgart one old German refuses to kneel and tells him there are always men like him.

Two brothers out of television comedy turned the Captain America sequel into a 1970s paranoia thriller and inherited the saga: Joe and Anthony Russo. They cast Robert Redford partly as an homage to his own thrillers of that decade, above all the hunted analyst of Three Days of the Condor. James Gunn's abducted Earth boy carries his dead mother's cassette everywhere, labelled Awesome Mix Vol. 1. His crew of misfits, raccoon and walking tree included, are the Guardians of the Galaxy. The tree, voiced by Vin Diesel, is Groot.

Age of Ultron adds a synthetic man with the Mind Stone set in his forehead, Vision, played by Paul Bettany, Stark's computer voice since 2008. Rights deals forbade the word mutant for the Maximoff twins, so the film used their comic names, Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver. At the party the hammer twitches for one man, and four years later he swings it: Captain America.

A ruined neurosurgeon is chosen by a relic that thinks for itself, the Cloak of Levitation. Michael Keaton's salvager builds a winged suit out of alien scrap: the Vulture. Ben Kingsley's dreadful Mandarin turns out to be a drug-addled British actor called Trevor Slattery, hired as a face. Taika Waititi, out of New Zealand, scrapped the solemn Thor tone and voiced the rock gladiator Korg himself. Led Zeppelin, which almost never licenses its songs, cleared Immigrant Song only after the band saw the first cut of the trailer.

Vibranium-rich Wakanda and its cat-suited king carry the 2018 film Black Panther. The shaven-headed spearwomen guarding him were modelled on a real regiment, the Agojie of Dahomey, who fought from the seventeenth century until the French broke them in the 1890s. The exiled cousin Killmonger is played by Michael B. Jordan, whom the director had already used in Fruitvale Station and Creed. What finally splits Stark from Rogers in Civil War is 1991 footage of the brainwashed Bucky Barnes killing Stark's parents for Hydra.

The warlord from Titan who gathers all six stones to wipe out half of life is Thanos. Vormir's gatekeeper demands a soul, so he throws his adopted daughter Gamora off the cliff. When the snap lands, the teenage Spider-Man comes apart in Stark's arms, stammering that he does not feel so good. Endgame opens with Thor finding him retired on a farm and taking his head off with Stormbreaker, going for the head this time. The heist sets Rogers against himself in 2012, and he wins with two words about Bucky being alive. On Vormir the price falls due again, and the one who jumps is Natasha Romanoff. The 1995 prequel had already inverted the comics: the shapeshifting Skrulls are refugees fleeing a genocide and the Kree are the aggressors. Falcon's voice reaches Rogers by radio with their old running joke, telling him to look on his left. Rogers lifts Mjolnir and speaks the two words held back for twenty-two films: Avengers, assemble. Stark drags the stones onto his own glove and closes the saga with his four words from 2008, that he is Iron Man.

harry-potter.context_blurb:
The letter comes at eleven, the scarlet engine leaves King's Cross from Platform Nine and Three-Quarters, and the castle at the end of the line has four ancient houses. Its full name is Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

Joanne Rowling thought of the orphan wizard on a delayed Manchester train in 1990 and wrote the book broke, in Edinburgh cafés: J.K. Rowling. Twelve publishers turned it down before a small London house, Bloomsbury, took it because its chief executive's eight-year-old daughter called it so much better than anything else. The British title is Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone; American shelves got a different word.

The pale, snake-faced wizard who murdered Harry's parents and split his soul to cheat death is Voldemort. The headmaster in half-moon spectacles who beat Grindelwald in 1945 is Albus Dumbledore. The half-giant gamekeeper who kicks the Dursleys' door down with the letter is Rubeus Hagrid. His birthday present to Harry is a snowy owl, Hedwig. The Muggle-born girl who saves them all by reading is Hermione Granger. The Sorting Hat gives Harry the house he asks for: Gryffindor. The serpent house was founded by Salazar Slytherin. The house of earth and loyalty is Hufflepuff, and the relic Helga left behind is a small golden cup. The greasy Potions master who torments Harry for years while secretly serving Dumbledore is Severus Snape. Quidditch gives Harry the job of hunting the golden Snitch, which makes him a Seeker.

In the Chamber of Secrets he kills the basilisk, then drives a fang through the object possessing Ginny: Tom Riddle's diary. Dumbledore later gives such soul-containers their name, Horcruxes. In Prisoner of Azkaban the escaped convict proves to be Harry's framed godfather, Sirius Black, whose Animagus shape is a great black dog they called Padfoot. Hagrid's first lesson brings out a proud eagle-horse, the Hippogriff Buckbeak. Hermione's impossible timetable runs on a tiny gold hourglass, a Time-Turner. The Marauder's Map opens on a solemn promise of being up to no good and shuts again with mischief managed. Alfonso Cuarón directed the third film and set the darker look the rest copied: Prisoner of Azkaban.

The Triwizard trophy is a Portkey: it drops Harry and Cedric in a graveyard where Voldemort comes back. That ritual needs bone of the father, flesh of the servant, and blood of the enemy, taken from Harry by force. The Defence teacher that year was an imposter on hourly Polyjuice, the Death Eater Barty Crouch Jr. The wizarding rock band that plays the Yule Ball is the Weird Sisters.

Dolores Umbridge bans real spellwork, so the students drill in secret as Dumbledore's Army. Hermione finally lures her into the Forbidden Forest, where the centaurs carry her off. Rowling has described Umbridge as a blend of people she had met, among them an instructor she disliked on sight. Sirius dies falling backwards through the stone archway in the Death Chamber, the Veil. In the Ministry duel Fawkes swallows the killing curse meant for Dumbledore. A phoenix's own feathers are crimson and gold.

The annotated potions book signed by the Half-Blood Prince belonged to Snape, whose mother was Eileen Prince. Only the Bloody Baron, the Slytherin ghost, can make Peeves behave. The wandmaker at 1 Diagon Alley, Garrick Ollivander, sells Harry a wand whose phoenix-feather core has a twin in the wand that scarred him.

The first brother's wand in the wizarding fairy tale of three brothers is the Elder Wand. Voldemort never truly masters it, because Draco disarmed Dumbledore on the tower and Harry later disarmed Draco. Hermione wipes from her parents the memory that they ever had a daughter, and renames them Wendell and Monica Wilkins. Ron finds his way back with the Deluminator Dumbledore left him. Hermione destroys Hufflepuff's cup down in the Chamber with a basilisk fang. The Black family's bitter old house-elf is Kreacher. The twin killed mid-laugh in the Battle of Hogwarts is Fred Weasley. Dumbledore asks if he loves Lily even now, and Snape answers in a single word: always. Under a bench in the King's Cross chapter lies a flayed, child-sized thing, the remnant of Voldemort's soul.

Becoming an Animagus means holding a Mandrake leaf in the mouth for a whole month. Harry's own Patronus comes out in his father's shape, a stag. The Potters were given away by the Secret-Keeper they swapped in at the last minute, Peter Pettigrew. The Mirror of Erised says backwards that it shows not your face but your heart's desire.

pokemon-franchise.context_blurb:
Pokemon grew out of a boy's beetle-hunting in Machida: Satoshi Tajiri. His Game Freak co-founder, who has drawn every monster since, is Ken Sugimori. Red and Green reached Japan in February 1996 with 151 creatures in the first dex. The region modelled on east-central Japan is Kanto. A new trainer's hometown there is Pallet Town. Wild Pokemon are caught with a red-and-white Pokeball. Eight Kanto gym badges open the Indigo Plateau.

Giovanni's Viridian gym hands over the Earth Badge. Lavender's haunted building is the Pokemon Tower, and the ghost inside cannot even be seen without the Silph Scope. Cubone wears his own dead mother's skull. The Vermilion gym leader's evolved ace is Raichu. Articuno sits at the lowest floor of the Seafoam Islands. The cloned legendary of Cinnabar is Mewtwo. The mansion journals that tell his story begin with a new Pokemon found in the jungles of Guyana. The first film has him blast the island laboratory that made him. Charizard's second type beside Fire is Flying. The Pokedex warns that Charmander dies if his tail flame ever goes out. The cover star of Blue, in Japan and America alike, is Blastoise. The anime tie-in version that starts the player with Pikachu is Pokemon Yellow.

The anime's yellow mascot is Pikachu. Ikue Ōtani voices Pikachu in every language, which no other Pokemon's actor does. Team Rocket's talking cat is Meowth, and Jessie opens their rhyming motto with prepare for trouble. Meowth learned to talk to impress a female Meowth. Their Japanese names, Musashi and Kojiro, come from two famous duelling swordsmen, Miyamoto Musashi and Sasaki Kojiro. Misty's glamorous older trio bill themselves as the Sensational Sisters. She follows Ash because Pikachu fried her bicycle. Brock's rock-snake ace, soaked by the gym sprinklers, is Onix. Jigglypuff's lullaby sends all its listeners to sleep, so it scribbles on their faces with its microphone marker. Blaine, the riddle-door fire leader, keeps his gym on Cinnabar Island. Sabrina shares her gym with her father and a doll holding her own childhood self. Delia's housekeeping helper is Mr. Mime. Ash's first wild catch on Route 1 is a Caterpie, set free as a Butterfree in the episode called Bye Bye Butterfree. The digital Pokemon banned after the seizure episode is Porygon. The end-credits song that names all 151 is the Pokerap. Jason Paige sang the English theme.

Charmander's first trainer, who left him on a rock in the rain, was Damian. Charmeleon evolved in mid-flight chasing the Aerodactyl that had snatched Ash. As a Charizard he stopped obeying, judging Ash too weak to command a fully evolved Pokemon. Tad's Poliwrath once froze him with Ice Beam, and Ash stayed up all night keeping him warm. His finisher, grabbing an opponent and slamming him down, is Seismic Toss. Ritchie's Pikachu is Sparky, and his Charmander is Zippo.

The English Base Set, printed in 1999 by Wizards of the Coast, has one holographic prize above all: Charizard. The dearest printing is 1st Edition Shadowless. The rarest card of all, awarded in a CoroCoro illustration contest, is Pikachu Illustrator. Gold and Silver added a working clock and a new region west of Kanto, Johto. That clock battery sits soldered to the cartridge board behind a Tri-wing screw, and it has died in most carts. HeartGold and SoulSilver brought back a Pokemon walking behind the player. Pokemon Snap's young photographer is Todd Snap. Pokemon Stadium's button-pattern minigame is Clefairy Says. Niantic's 2016 walking game is Pokemon GO. Mega Charizard X drops Flying and becomes Fire and Dragon. The actor behind Deadpool voiced the 2019 live-action Pikachu: Ryan Reynolds. Cutting the National Dex out of Sword and Shield earned the nickname Dexit.

The Old Man on the Viridian docks writes the player's name into the data the game later reads as a species. Surfing the Cinnabar coast then spawns Missingno. Saving and re-entering the Safari Zone drops the player into Glitch City. Playground rumour put Mew under the parked truck beside the dock. One real giveaway ran at Toys R Us stores at the end of 1999. The anime gave Ash Pikachu instead of a starter on purpose, since any one starter would have opened a gap with every child who had picked a different one. Smash's Pokemon Trainer wears the backwards cap of Red, the silent hero of the Game Boy games.

movie-misc-classics.context_blurb:
Three films out of one decade, connected by nothing except the way people still argue about them.

Ron Howard grew up on American television as the red-headed boy on The Andy Griffith Show and then went behind the camera. In 1985 he made Cocoon, in which a group of Florida retirees climb into a neighbour's swimming pool, find alien pods glowing at the bottom of it, and climb out feeling thirty years younger. The year before that he had directed Disney's first grown-up release under its Touchstone label, a mermaid comedy with Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah: Splash. Don Ameche, a leading man of the 1930s, won Best Supporting Actor for Cocoon at the age of seventy-seven, and in the film's show-stopping scene he breakdances across a nightclub floor, though a double did most of the dancing.

Martin Scorsese's Goodfellas, in 1990, puts Ray Liotta in the shoes of Henry Hill, a real Lucchese-family mobster who spent decades in the New York rackets. The screenplay grew out of hundreds of taped interviews the journalist Nicholas Pileggi had recorded with Hill for a book published in 1985, Wiseguy: Life in a Mafia Family. The film could not keep that title, because a television series called Wiseguy was on the air at the time.

John Carpenter's The Thing opened in June 1982, two weeks behind E.T., and sank at the box office, with a critical shrug that took decades to reverse. An Antarctic research crew digs up a shape-shifter that can copy any living thing it touches, so that no man can trust the man beside him, and a designer barely into his twenties, Rob Bottin, built the creatures by hand out of rubber, slime and hidden machinery, working until he landed in hospital with exhaustion, double pneumonia and a bleeding ulcer.

cryptids-folk-monsters-and-internet-lege.context_blurb:
Cryptids are creatures that eyewitnesses and legends describe but science has never confirmed. Their stories come from old folk traditions, famous photographs and, lately, internet fiction.

The Navajo tell of the skinwalker, a witch who becomes a coyote, wolf or crow, and many will not say its name aloud. The Cree, Ojibwe and other Algonquian peoples feared the wendigo, a gaunt winter spirit of famine that hungers for human flesh. People convinced they were becoming one are now described as having a culture-bound syndrome, shaped by famine, isolation and the Algonquian horror of cannibalism. Sherpas of the Himalayas spoke of the Yeti for centuries before Western climbers reported giant footprints. In Australia, many Aboriginal nations tell of a shaggy giant called the Yowie. Legend says New Jersey's Pine Barrens hide the Jersey Devil, a hoofed, bat-winged horror whose own mother cursed it at birth. Historian Brian Regal traced the name to the Leeds family of Burlington County: Daniel Leeds, a Quaker surveyor and almanac-maker, filled his almanacs with astrology until fellow Quakers branded him a heretic.

Bigfoot is said to roam the rainy forests of the Pacific Northwest. Its older name, Sasquatch, is Salish; a reporter coined Bigfoot in 1958, after logger Jerry Crew brought plaster casts of giant prints to a California paper. In 1967 Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin filmed a figure they took for a female Bigfoot crossing a creek sandbar, and Patterson nicknamed it Patty. Frame 352, where the figure glances back at the camera, is the most reprinted image. Bob Heironimus later claimed he wore the suit, a modified horsehide costume over a football helmet. Creature-suit maker Bill Munns studied scans of the film and argued no 1967 costume could move like that.

Scotland's Loch Ness has a legendary monster, known worldwide as Nessie. The loch is about 754 feet deep and so stained by peat that divers see only a few feet. Her most famous image, the 1934 Surgeon's Photograph, shows a small head on a long neck. People trusted it because its supposed taker, Robert Kenneth Wilson, was a respected gynecologist. In 1994, near death, Christian Spurling admitted that his stepfather, big-game hunter Marmaduke Wetherell, staged it to get back at the Daily Mail for mocking his fake footprints. The monster was a toy submarine from Woolworth's with a putty neck.

Lake Champlain, between Vermont and New York, is said to hide Champ; Samuel de Champlain wrote of a strange creature there. Its best-known photo, Sandra Mansi's 1977 Polaroid, cannot be tested: a Polaroid has no negative, and she lost the camera and the exact spot. Canada's Ogopogo is said to swim in British Columbia's Lake Okanagan.

In 1995, after Puerto Rican sheep turned up dead with their blood apparently drained, a radio host named the unseen attacker the chupacabra, the goat-sucker. On Zanzibar, panics over the bat-winged Popobawa come in waves; anthropologist Martin Walsh found they swell at elections and in political tension, a culture-bound mass anxiety. In 1983 the cousins Frances Griffiths and Elsie Wright admitted that their fairies, which had fooled Arthur Conan Doyle, were paper cutouts traced from a children's book and held up with hatpins.

Virginia has Bunny Man Bridge, officially the Colchester Overpass, where legend says a hatchet-swinging man in a rabbit suit lurks; two real 1970 police reports started the tale. Kentucky's Pope Lick trestle has a goatman legend and a real danger: trains still cross it, and at least eight climbers have died.

Slender Man, the faceless giant in a dark suit, began in 2009 as Eric Knudsen's entry in a photo-editing contest on the Something Awful forums. Journalist Brian Bethel started the Black-Eyed Kids in 1996 with a post saying two black-eyed boys came to his car in Texas. The SCP Foundation wiki began in 2007 with SCP-173, a statue that moves only when unwatched. The Backrooms began in 2019 on 4chan with one photo of an empty yellow office. Its caption set the horror in the details: an endless fluorescent hum and the faint smell of damp carpet.

Memory builds legends too. Fiona Broome coined the Mandela Effect for people sure that Mandela had died in prison. In fact Nelson Mandela walked free in 1990, became president of South Africa in 1994, and died in December 2013. Psychologists blame the brain, which rebuilds a memory each time it recalls one.

ancient-mysteries-and-lost-worlds.context_blurb:
Some mysteries are older than any history book: a drowned empire in a Greek dialogue, stone giants on a Pacific island, a bronze computer from a shipwreck, a book nobody can read. Others are only four centuries old, like an English colony that vanished from the American coast.

Plato described Atlantis around 360 BC as a proud island empire out past the Strait of Gibraltar, in the Atlantic Ocean, which the gods drowned within one day and night. Stonehenge, the ring of giant slabs on Salisbury Plain in the south of England, is more than four thousand years old. In Egypt, the Great Pyramid rose as Pharaoh Khufu's tomb around 2560 BC, and its size and precision still breed wild theories about its builders. In the 1990s Robert Bauval argued that the three Giza pyramids copy the pattern of the three stars of Orion's Belt, a precise match most Egyptologists reject. On Rapa Nui, the island outsiders call Easter Island, Polynesian carvers cut almost nine hundred stone giants called moai. In Peru's Nazca Desert, people scraped away dark stones to draw a hummingbird, a monkey and miles of lines so vast that the figures can only be seen whole from the air. In 1901 sponge divers off the Greek island of Antikythera hauled up a crust of green bronze from a Roman-era wreck, now called the Antikythera Mechanism. The Voynich Manuscript, six centuries old, is crowded with unknown plants, star charts and bathing women, captioned in a script that nobody has ever managed to read or translate. It is kept today in the rare-book library of Yale University.

In 1587 English settlers landed on Roanoke Island, and when Governor John White got back with supplies in 1590 every one was gone; the only clue was the word Croatoan, cut into a post. Among the lost was his baby granddaughter, Virginia Dare, the first child of English parents born in the future United States.

Plato told the Atlantis tale in two late dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, crediting it to Solon, who heard it from a priest in Egypt; most classicists read it as Plato's own parable about a proud sea power. Archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos argued in 1939 that a Bronze Age eruption on Thera, the island now called Santorini, had wrecked Minoan Crete, and later that memories of the blast lay behind Atlantis; his dig at Akrotiri uncovered a whole town under its ash.

In 1995 Klaus Schmidt began digging Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey: rings of carved pillars raised around 9500 BC, before farming reached the region, a hint, Schmidt argued, that worship came before fields.

Months after the Antikythera find, the drying lump split open in an Athens museum to show a wooden case with bronze gears and Greek writing on its edges. X-rays later revealed dozens of hand-cut gears that modeled the sky, predicting the positions of sun, moon and planets and the coming of eclipses. A spiral dial followed the Babylonian saros cycle of 223 lunar months, which holds about 51 eclipses, so each cycle's eclipses foretold the next.

Rapa Nui tradition said the moai walked to their platforms, and in 2012 Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo showed how: three rope teams rocked a replica from side to side while hauling it forward, so it waddled upright. Their book, The Statues That Walked, also rejected the old story that the islanders ruined their own island, blaming imported disease and slave raids instead.

Stonehenge's smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills of southwest Wales, about 150 miles away. In 2015 Mike Parker Pearson's team traced them to two quarries, Carn Goedog for spotted dolerite and Craig Rhos-y-felin for rhyolite.

The Voynich Manuscript is named for Wilfrid Voynich, the book dealer who bought it from Jesuits outside Rome in 1912. Yale files it as MS 408 and has put every page online so anyone can attack the code. William Friedman, the codebreaker who cracked Japan's Purple cipher, spent decades on it and concluded it was an early attempt at a constructed philosophical language.

From 1937 dozens of carved Dare Stones turned up, claiming to tell how the Roanoke colonists survived, until a 1941 magazine investigation showed the later ones were the work of a stonecutter named Bill Eberhardt, who sold them to Brenau College in Georgia.

On Nova Scotia's Oak Island, treasure hunters have dug the Money Pit since 1795, and the early diggers reported log platforms roughly every 10 feet down the shaft before it flooded.

ancient-mysteries-and-lost-worlds.title: Ancient Mysteries and Lost Worlds

ufos-close-encounters-and-cold-war-secre.context_blurb:
Since the flying-saucer summer of 1947, Americans have watched the skies and wondered what their government was hiding. Some sightings found plain answers, and some stay unexplained.

In July 1947 the Army airfield at Roswell, New Mexico, boasted of capturing a crashed flying disc, then called it a weather balloon. In 1994 the Air Force named the real wreckage: Project Mogul, secret balloons with microphones to catch the pressure waves of Soviet atomic tests. Area 51, where the Air Force tests spy planes, lies in the Nevada desert.

In 1908 a fireball exploded in mid-air over Siberia in Russia, flattening some eighty million trees but leaving no crater. Mineralogist Leonid Kulik led the first expedition in 1927 and found trees blown outward in a butterfly pattern, the central ones standing but bare. That pattern means the blast struck from above: a stony asteroid burst some 5 to 10 kilometers up.

In August 1977 Ohio State's Big Ear radio telescope, built to search for signals from outer space, caught a narrow burst that lasted seventy-two seconds and was never heard again. The printout logged its strength as the characters 6EQUJ5, where letters meant readings above nine and U, about thirty times the background, was the peak. Jerry Ehman circled it and wrote Wow! beside it. Big Ear itself is gone, dismantled in 1998 so that developers could expand a nearby golf course. It came near 1420 MHz, the hydrogen line, which scientists guessed aliens would use because hydrogen is the commonest element in the universe.

In 1952 a group in Flatwoods, West Virginia, reported a glowing-headed giant that newspapers named the Flatwoods Monster; skeptics say they saw a meteor, then a startled barn owl. In 1955 two Kentucky farm families said they fired hundreds of rounds at silvery goblins that would not fall; Joe Nickell argued they were great horned owls defending their nest.

The abduction story was born in the 1960s, when Betty and Barney Hill said a disc chased their car through New Hampshire in 1961. Betty's dreams came first and led a Boston doctor to hypnotize the couple. Betty drew a star map she said the aliens had shown her, which teacher Marjorie Fish matched to Zeta Reticuli; Carl Sagan was a sharp critic, and Fish later gave up the match.

From 1966 people in Point Pleasant, West Virginia, reported the Mothman, a winged, red-eyed figure seen most around the TNT Area, a deserted wartime explosives plant just outside town. When the Silver Bridge across the Ohio River fell at rush hour in December 1967, forty-six people died. A tiny crack in one eyebar of the north chain on the Ohio side caused it; the chain had no backup. John Keel tied the sightings to the disaster in his 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies.

In 1975 Travis Walton's crew, thinning trees on a US Forest Service contract in Arizona's Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest, said a glowing craft zapped him and he vanished. He turned up five days later, and his story became the 1993 film Fire in the Sky. In 1997 a silent V of lights crossed Phoenix; the leading plain explanation is A-10 Warthogs of the Maryland Air National Guard, plus training flares.

Some secrets were real. From the 1950s the CIA ran MKUltra, testing whether drugs and hypnosis could control minds, and its chemist Sidney Gottlieb dosed unwitting people with LSD. Days after Gottlieb secretly dosed Army biochemist Frank Olson with LSD in 1953, Olson fell, or was pushed, through a window of New York's Hotel Statler, now the Hotel Pennsylvania. Numbers stations, flat voices reading digits on shortwave radio, are widely believed to send one-way coded messages to spies in the field.

In Utah the Sherman family bought Skinwalker Ranch in 1994 and reported glowing orbs and mutilated cattle; two years later aerospace billionaire Robert Bigelow bought it. The Pentagon later paid a Bigelow company to study the ranch under AAWSAP, an effort later known as AATIP, the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program. Its main report on the ranch is often called the BAASS Skinwalker Ranch Report.

Crop circles turned out human: in 1991 Doug Bower and Dave Chorley showed reporters the plank and rope they had used to flatten English wheat since 1978. Pattern-hunting does the rest: of the famous Lincoln-Kennedy coincidences, one of the few true ones is that both slain presidents were succeeded by vice presidents named Johnson.

vanishings-ghost-ships-and-cold-cases.context_blurb:
Some mysteries begin with an empty space: a ship with no crew, a lighthouse with no keepers, a hijacker who stepped into the sky. Others begin with a body and no answer, and few are truly closed.

In December 1872 sailors found the Mary Celeste drifting east of the Azores, sails set, cargo untouched, lifeboat gone. Her captain, Benjamin Briggs, his wife, their small daughter and seven crewmen were never seen again. The best-defended theory blames her cargo of 1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol: nine were empty, and Briggs may have feared the leaking fumes would explode and ordered everyone into the boat. In 1900 a relief ship found the Flannan Isles Lighthouse off Scotland empty, its three keepers gone and a clock stopped; a freak storm wave most likely took them.

The Bermuda Triangle, a patch of the North Atlantic Ocean framed by Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico, owes its fame to writers; statistics show no more losses there than in other busy waters. Its most famous loss is Flight 19, five Navy Grumman TBM Avengers lost on a 1945 training flight. Vincent Gaddis coined the name in 1964, and Charles Berlitz's 1974 bestseller made it famous. The Philadelphia Experiment, the tale that the Navy made the warship USS Eldridge invisible in 1943, dies on the ship's own logs: the Eldridge was not at the Philadelphia Navy Yard that October, and no invisibility test ever happened. In 2014 Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 vanished with 239 people aboard; satellite pings traced it to the southern Indian Ocean.

On Thanksgiving Eve 1971 a hijacker calling himself Dan Cooper collected two hundred thousand dollars and four parachutes in Seattle, then parachuted from the plane's rear stairs into a stormy night. After copycats tried the same exit, the FAA had every Boeing 727 fitted with a small airflow wedge that locks those stairs in flight, the Cooper vane. In 1980 young Brian Ingram dug three rotting packets of the ransom out of a Columbia River sandbar, the only money ever found. Sleuths led by Tom Kaye later found cerium, strontium sulfide and specks of pure titanium on the clip-on tie Cooper left behind, a mix pointing to aerospace work such as Boeing's supersonic airliner project.

In February 1959 nine Soviet hikers slit their tent open from inside and fled to their deaths in the northern Ural Mountains, at what is now Dyatlov Pass. Some had crushing injuries. Almost all were students at the Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk, a school that trained engineers for Soviet nuclear work. Radiation traces on some of the clothing probably have an ordinary explanation, thorium from the gas-lantern mantles the hikers handled, and a Russian inquiry reopened in 2019 blamed an avalanche for the panic.

In 1948 the Somerton Man, a stranger with every clothing label cut away, lay dead on a beach near Adelaide with a scrap reading Tamam Shud, torn from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, in a hidden pocket. In 2022 Derek Abbott used DNA from a hair in a plaster bust to name him as Carl Webb, an electrical engineer from Melbourne.

Jack the Ripper's first accepted victim, killed in Whitechapel in August 1888, was Mary Ann Nichols, known as Polly. In 1892 someone took a hatchet to Andrew Borden, a Fall River banker, and his wife; his daughter Lizzie Borden was tried and acquitted, and a skipping rhyme keeps her name alive. The Zodiac Killer's 340-character cipher was finally cracked in 2020, and it held only a taunt that he was not afraid of the gas chamber. In 1966 two Brazilian technicians were found dead on Morro do Vintém wearing lead masks beside a note about swallowing capsules and awaiting a signal.

The oldest case began in 1483, when the boy-king Edward V and his brother vanished in the Tower of London after their uncle took the throne as Richard III. Henry Tudor defeated Richard at Bosworth in 1485 and became Henry VII. Richard's grave was lost for five centuries until a 2012 Leicester University dig found his bones under a municipal car park behind the city council offices.

dnd-gygax-tsr-and-the-satanic-panic.context_blurb:
Dungeons & Dragons was born in the American Midwest in the early 1970s, when two wargamers turned battles of toy soldiers into a game of heroes exploring dungeons. Its history runs through a tiny company's rise and fall, a shelf of famous rulebooks, and a moral panic.

Gary Gygax had co-written Chainmail, a 1971 medieval war game for tabletop miniatures, and Dave Arneson of Minneapolis built his Blackmoor campaign on it, bringing in the dungeon crawl and the referee. In 1974 Gygax's little company, TSR, published the new game from Lake Geneva, Wisconsin, the lakeside town where he spent his adult life. He had founded TSR the year before with his childhood friend Don Kaye, the two of them pooling $2,400 to start it; Kaye suffered a fatal heart attack at thirty-six, in January 1975. Kaye's death forced a reorganization, and late that year the firm became TSR Hobbies, Inc., keeping the old initials. The first print run was just one thousand boxes, early ones assembled by hand in Gygax's basement. Each held three booklets, Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures. Gygax had also co-founded Gen Con in 1968, a gaming meet in Lake Geneva whose name was his pun on the Geneva Convention.

The original white box offered three classes, the Fighting-Man, the Magic-User and the healing Cleric, a crusading vampire-hunter meant to keep one of Arneson's vampires in check. In 1975 the Greyhawk supplement added a fourth, the sneaky Thief, who could climb walls, pick locks and backstab. The 1976 Eldritch Wizardry supplement brought the druid and psionic combat, mental powers such as telepathy that many referees banned. From 1977 to 1979 Gygax rebuilt the game as Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, in three big hardcovers. The first of them, the 1977 Monster Manual, was the first hardcover D&D rulebook, a leap from the pamphlets and boxed booklets that came before. The art of that era took its weird, bright, psychedelic edge from Erol Otus, a TSR staff artist by 1979 who painted the cover of the 1981 Basic Set.

From June 1976, TSR's Dragon Magazine brought monsters and rules debates to fans for 359 issues, until 2007. From 1987 to 2004 its Sage Advice column answered readers' rules puzzles through Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition.

For beginners, TSR in 1977 issued a blue Basic box edited by J. Eric Holmes, a California neurologist and science-fiction writer. Tom Moldvay's 1981 and Frank Mentzer's 1983 versions followed, and Mentzer's grew into five boxes named Basic, Expert, Companion, Master and Immortals, BECMI for short, which carried heroes all the way to godhood. In 1991 Aaron Allston gathered the Basic through Master rules into one hardcover, the Rules Cyclopedia, which fans praise as the cleanest D&D book ever.

In 1985 Gygax was pushed out of his own company by Lorraine Williams, the general manager he had hired, who bought up enough shares to outvote him. Under her, TSR sank into debt, and in 1997 Williams sold it to Wizards of the Coast, made rich by its card game Magic: The Gathering.

The Satanic Panic took off in 1979, when a Michigan State student of sixteen, James Dallas Egbert III, went missing in the university's steam tunnels and a private detective blamed D&D. The truth was sadder and had little to do with the game: Egbert was a troubled boy, and his gaming group was an outlet for him, not the cause of his trouble. His story inspired the 1982 TV film Mazes and Monsters, starring a young Tom Hanks, a future Oscar winner, in his first lead role. Hanks played Robbie Wheeling, a student who loses himself in his game character, the holy man Pardieu. Steven Hilliard Stern directed it for CBS, from Tom Lazarus's script of Rona Jaffe's novel. In 1983 Patricia Pulling, who blamed the game for her teenage son's death, founded B.A.D.D., Bothered About Dungeons & Dragons. In 1984 Jack Chick, maker of tiny evangelical comic tracts, published Dark Dungeons, in which a game master lures a girl named Debbie into real witchcraft. Debbie then casts a Mind Bondage spell on her father, who has been trying to stop her playing, a spell Chick invented that appears in no D&D book.

The game reached Saturday mornings too: from 1983 CBS aired a cartoon simply titled Dungeons & Dragons, in which six kids are swept into the Realm and hunted by the sorcerer Venger.

dnd-classic-monsters-and-the-underdark.context_blurb:
Classic Dungeons & Dragons stocked its dungeons from everywhere: Greek myth, pulp science fiction, a bag of dime-store toys, and the imaginations of Gary Gygax and his players. Many of the strangest lived deep underground, in a lightless world ruled by dark elves and their spider goddess.

Some came straight from Greek myth: Pegasus, the winged horse Bellerophon rode; the riddling Sphinx that guarded Thebes until Oedipus answered her; and the Chimera, part lion, part goat and part serpent. The Lich is a wizard who cheats death by sealing his soul in a hidden jar called a phylactery, so smashing his body only sends him home to it. The most feared lich, Vecna, was created by Brian Blume and shrank over the ages to one hand and one eye that give terrible power to anyone who attaches them; his name is an anagram of Jack Vance, whose fantasy stories shaped the game's magic. Demogorgon, the Prince of Demons, has two snarling baboon heads, tentacles for arms and bat wings. Against Tiamat, the five-headed queen of the evil chromatic dragons, stands Bahamut, the platinum god of the good metallic dragons, who sometimes walks the world as a robed old man.

Others came from a bag of cheap plastic toy monsters that Gygax kept on his desk. One became the feathered, beaked Owlbear, kept just as the toy looked. Another became the Rust Monster, whose touch crumbles even a magic sword to dust. A third became the finned, burrowing bulette, which players nicknamed the landshark. The Gelatinous Cube is a block of clear jelly exactly ten feet on a side, the width of a standard corridor, so it sweeps the passages clean, dissolving everything organic and leaving coins and steel behind. The six-legged, tentacled Displacer Beast, whose image always hangs a little to one side of its true body, was borrowed from the coeurl, a monster in a 1939 story by the science-fiction writer Van Vogt. Monster Manual II, published in 1983, added the Tarrasque, a doomsday colossus named for a dragon of Provence that Saint Martha tamed, which in the first rules only a wish could finish off.

Gygax himself created the Mind Flayer in 1975, the purple, octopus-headed villain that stuns heroes with psychic blasts and eats their brains, partly inspired by the tentacles on the cover of a Brian Lumley horror novel. The 1976 psionics rules brought another mind-eater, the Intellect Devourer, a walking brain on four legs.

The beholder was dreamed up by Terry Kuntz, the brother of Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-referee, and Gygax wrote it up for the rules. The floating eye tyrant first appeared in 1975 in the Greyhawk supplement, which shows it on the cover. Each of its ten eyestalks shoots its own ray, from sleep and charm to disintegration. Its huge central eye shuts off magic in a cone spreading out in front of it, so a spell cast from behind or the side still lands.

Far beneath the surface lies the Underdark, home of the Drow, the dark elves with coal-black skin and white hair who abandoned the daylight ages ago. They worship Lolth, a cruel spider goddess who can take the shape of a vast spider wearing a woman's face, and who rewards betrayal from the Demonweb Pits, her layer of the Abyss. Gygax's 1978 module Vault of the Drow first showed their city, Erelhei-Cinlu, set in the Vault, a cavern miles wide under a ceiling that glitters like a starry sky. That adventure path ended in 1980 with Q1 Queen of the Demonweb Pits, where heroes confront Lolth on her own plane of the Abyss. Her reach extends to the surface too: in Gygax's Village of Hommlet the bandit chief of the ruined moathouse is Lareth the Beautiful, a young evil priest favored by Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders.

dnd-greyhawk-ravenloft-and-classic-modul.context_blurb:
Gary Gygax ran his own games in a world he called Greyhawk, and many of the most famous early adventures, sold as thin booklets called modules, began at his table. Ravenloft added a gothic vampire tale that grew into a whole land of horror.

The most famous of Gygax's own characters, played from 1972, was the wizard Mordenkainen of Oerth, who rose to lead the Circle of Eight and lent his name to spells such as a magnificent mansion and a faithful hound. The other famous archwizards were characters from the same games, mostly run by his players: Tenser was played by Gygax's son Ernie, Rary was Brian Blume's, and Drawmij was Jim Ward's, his name spelled backward. Bigby began as an evil wizard in the dungeons of Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and an early TSR employee, until Mordenkainen subdued him and Gygax took him over as a player character. Castle Greyhawk, where the game was first tested, was the original megadungeon, thirteen levels deep at first. In 1983 the world went into a boxed set, the World of Greyhawk Fantasy Game Setting, with a beloved map of the Flanaess painted by Darlene Pekul, credited simply as Darlene. The world's dark lord is Iuz, half-demon son of Graz'zt and the witch Iggwilv, a demigod ruling the Empire of Iuz in the north. Gygax also wrote novels about Gord the Rogue, a street thief from Greyhawk's Slum Quarter who rises to greatness; TSR printed the first two, and the rest came out after it pushed Gygax out at the end of 1985.

Tomb of Horrors began as Gygax's dungeon for a 1975 convention, built to humble players who boasted their heroes could beat any challenge, and in 1978 it appeared as S1, the first of the Special series. At its heart waits the demilich Acererak, a floating skull with jeweled eyes. Its most infamous trap is a green devil face whose open mouth is a sphere of annihilation: anyone who climbs in is disintegrated instantly, with no saving throw. Survivors learned to prod every flagstone with a ten-foot pole. Lawrence Schick's 1979 White Plume Mountain sends heroes after three stolen weapons, the trident Wave, the hammer Whelm and the greatsword Blackrazor. In Gygax's Expedition to the Barrier Peaks, published in 1980 as S3, a mountain cave turns out to be the way into a crashed spacecraft from the stars, where working robots, access cards in many colors and blaster rifles await. Gygax's 1978 giant series opened with G1 Steading of the Hill Giant Chief, a raid on a timber lodge where a feasting chieftain holds court. In 1980 the slaver series began with A1, Slave Pits of the Undercity, a hunt through a coastal city. Gygax's 1979 Village of Hommlet hid an evil cult, and its long-promised sequel arrived only in 1985 as the supermodule T1-4 The Temple of Elemental Evil.

For new players, B1 In Search of the Unknown came in the blue Basic box and taught referees to stock a dungeon themselves, leaving the monsters and treasure blank. Its successor, B2 The Keep on the Borderlands, took its place in the box from early 1980, shipped with every Moldvay Basic set, and sent beginners to a frontier fort beside the Caves of Chaos. The Expert set came with X1 The Isle of Dread, a tropical island of dinosaurs and lost tribes modeled on King Kong's Skull Island; the module also mapped the Known World used by later Basic adventures. Tracy and Laura Hickman's Desert of Desolation trilogy, published just before Ravenloft, opens with the ghost of the pharaoh Amun-Re, doomed to wander the sands until his tomb is robbed.

In 1983 Tracy Hickman and his wife Laura Hickman turned their Halloween home game into I6 Ravenloft, the castle of the vampire Strahd von Zarovich, who murdered his brother for love and was cursed to haunt it forever. Its most copied idea was a tarot-style card reading, drawn before play, that randomized Strahd's plans and where the key treasures lay, so no two games were alike. The 1990 Ravenloft setting grew into many domains, each ruled by a damned darklord and created by the Dark Powers, which drag evil souls in from across the multiverse.

dnd-campaign-worlds-novels-and-rival-rpg.context_blurb:
In the 1980s and 1990s TSR built whole new worlds for its game and sold millions of novels set in them, while rival companies invented their own kinds of role-playing. A player could fight dragons on Krynn, sail between the stars, or hunt the monsters of Lovecraft.

Dragonlance began as game modules in 1984, and when editor Margaret Weis teamed with Tracy Hickman to tell the story as novels, the first, Dragons of Autumn Twilight, quickly became a bestseller. Its most famous hero is Raistlin Majere, the frail, coughing, black-robed wizard twin of the warrior Caramon, whose golden hourglass eyes see everyone around him aging. Krynn's three moons rule its three orders of wizards, and the black moon Nuitari, unseen by all but its own followers, is the moon of the evil Black Robes. The age before the story ended in the Cataclysm, when the gods hurled a fiery mountain onto Istar to punish a Kingpriest who demanded godhood, and then withdrew from the world.

Ed Greenwood had been inventing his Forgotten Realms since boyhood, and in 1987 TSR released them as the Forgotten Realms Campaign Set, a gray box with two maps. In the 1989 Time of Troubles the overgod Ao cast the gods down to walk the land as mortals, because Bane and Myrkul had stolen the Tablets of Fate. The Realms' best-loved hero came from the novelist Salvatore. Drizzt Do'Urden, a kind-hearted dark elf who turned his back on Menzoberranzan, was slipped into The Crystal Shard in 1988 at the last minute as a sidekick, and stole the spotlight. The hero Salvatore had meant to star was the young barbarian Wulfgar of the Tribe of the Elk. Drizzt fights with two magic scimitars: Twinkle, an elven blade, and Icingdeath, won from a slain white dragon's treasure and named after the beast. Salvatore later told the drow ranger's childhood in The Dark Elf Trilogy, made up of Homeland, Exile and Sojourn.

Spelljammer, in 1989, sent the game into space and gave it the Giff, hippo-headed soldiers in red coats and tricorn hats who live for military rank. Its ships fly by magical helms, and the finest helms are sold by the Arcane, towering blue-skinned merchants who trade across the crystal spheres. Planescape's city of Sigil, shaped like a hollow ring, holds tens of thousands of portals, constantly opening and closing, to every corner of the multiverse. It is ruled by the silent Lady of Pain, crowned with blades, and anyone who speaks her name is said to vanish. Dark Sun's desert world of Athas, where metal is so scarce that warriors fight with bone and obsidian, took its look from the painter Brom. Athas became a wasteland through defiling, arcane magic that drains the life from plants around the caster. Its city of Tyr is ruled by the Sorcerer-King Kalak, whose slaves are building him a great ziggurat. In Birthright, in 1995, players ruled kingdoms as heirs of slain gods on Cerilia, the northwestern continent of the world Aebrynis. The world of Basic D&D, long called the Known World, was named Mystara in 1991, and its Hollow World box hid preserved ancient cultures inside the planet.

Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu is named for a story Lovecraft wrote at home in Providence and published in 1928, and it borrows that story's tentacled god. Its designer, Sandy Petersen, later built levels for id Software's Doom and Quake. The game runs on Basic Roleplaying, the d100 percentile system Chaosium first built for RuneQuest, so every skill check is a roll of percentile dice. RuneQuest's world of Glorantha, with its dragon-newts and talking ducks, was the lifelong creation of Greg Stafford, Chaosium's founder. In Marc Miller's 1977 Traveller, characters served careers in four-year terms during creation and made survival rolls, so a hero could die before play began. Champions, in 1981, let players buy custom powers piece by piece with points, and its rules became the Hero System, used for many genres. Paranoia, a 1984 comedy set in a complex run by an insane Computer, opened with a famous warning to stay alert, trust no one and keep your laser handy. Its players are Troubleshooters, sent to hunt traitors while secretly being traitors themselves.

tolkien-inklings-and-arthurian-fantasy.context_blurb:
J.R.R. Tolkien was an Oxford professor of Old English who invented languages, then myths for them to live in. His books, his friends and older tales of King Arthur shaped modern high fantasy.

In 1937 Tolkien published The Hobbit, in which thirteen dwarves hire Bilbo Baggins, a comfortable, hairy-footed hobbit, as their burglar. They want their gold back from Smaug, the fire-breathing dragon who sleeps on the hoard inside the Lonely Mountain. It is the grey-bearded wizard Gandalf who sends Bilbo off, and who later leads the Fellowship of the Ring. Its first sentence, about a hobbit living in a hole in the ground, came to Tolkien while he was marking exam scripts. In 1937 Gollum stakes his ring on a riddle game; in 1947 Tolkien rewrote the chapter so that Gollum stakes only the way out.

In the long sequel the ring proves to be the One Ring of the Dark Lord Sauron, and Bilbo's young cousin Frodo Baggins agrees to carry it out of the Shire. It can be destroyed only in the fire where Sauron forged it, the volcano Mount Doom in Mordor. Tolkien disliked The Return of the King as the title of its final part, feeling it gave too much away, and wanted The War of the Ring.

At the Somme in 1916 Tolkien served as a signals officer, and two of the four friends at the heart of his school club, Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith, were killed that year. He said that Samwise Gamgee, Frodo's faithful servant, reflected the ordinary English soldiers, the privates and batmen he had served beside.

The languages came first: Quenya is the high speech of the Elves, with a Finnish and Latin ring, and Sindarin is their everyday tongue, modelled on Welsh and behind most Elvish names in the books. Both use his own script, the Tengwar, its letters grouped by sound, as seen in the Ring's inscription and on the doors of Moria. The Dwarves keep a harsher secret language, and at the Hornburg Gimli shouts its war-cry, Baruk Khazâd! Khazâd ai-mênu!, axes of the Dwarves, the Dwarves are upon you.

Tolkien said the doomed hero of The Children of Húrin grew partly from Kullervo, a hapless hero of Finland's Kalevala whom he had written about as a student. His oldest myths tell of the Silmarils, jewels made by the Elf Feanor to hold the light of the Two Trees of Valinor, Telperion and Laurelin. His son Christopher Tolkien edited those myths into The Silmarillion, published in 1977. Tolkien saw his wife Edith in Lúthien, the elf-maiden who loves the mortal Beren, and their Oxford grave bears both names, Beren for him and Lúthien for her.

In Oxford, Tolkien, Lewis and their friends called themselves the Inklings and met to read work aloud, often at the Eagle and Child pub. After a night walk with Lewis and Hugo Dyson in 1931, Tolkien put his argument that pagan myths point toward one true myth into a poem, Mythopoeia. His essay On Fairy-Stories coined eucatastrophe, the good catastrophe, for a story's sudden turn to joy. Leaf by Niggle, about a painter who never finishes his great picture of a tree, is often read as a portrait of Tolkien himself. In a vast 1951 letter to Milton Waldman, a publisher, he said that all his mythology is mainly concerned with Fall, Mortality, and the Machine. His 1936 Beowulf lecture praised the poem's Northern courage, which fights on when defeat is certain. He translated Pearl, a medieval dream poem in which a grieving father meets his lost daughter. His children received illustrated letters from Father Christmas, in which a clumsy Polar Bear causes most of the trouble. When Dungeons & Dragons borrowed his creatures, Tolkien's rights holders objected in 1977, so hobbits became halflings, ents became treants and balrogs became balors.

Tolkien's fantasy grew from older Arthurian roots. Le Morte d'Arthur, which Thomas Malory completed about 1470, probably in prison, was known for centuries only through William Caxton's printed edition of 1485. White's The Once and Future King became the 1960 musical Camelot, with Richard Burton as Arthur. Mary Stewart's Merlin trilogy opens with The Crystal Cave, a name tied to Bryn Myrddin, Merlin's Hill, near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, where legend puts Merlin's cave. Marion Zimmer Bradley's The Mists of Avalon (1983) is narrated by Morgaine, the woman older tales call Morgan le Fay, a priestess of Avalon's goddess religion.

poe-lovecraft-and-weird-fiction.context_blurb:
Weird fiction is the horror of the unknown: ghosts, forbidden books and gods older than the stars. It runs from Edgar Allan Poe in the 1840s to Lovecraft and the pulp magazine Weird Tales a century later.

In Poe's poem The Raven (1845) a grieving man questions a black bird perched above his door, and it answers every question with one word, Nevermore. In The Tell-Tale Heart (1843) a killer who swears he is sane hides an old man under the floorboards, then thinks he hears the heart still beating. The Pit and the Pendulum (1843) binds a prisoner of the Spanish Inquisition beneath a swinging blade while hot iron walls close in. In The Fall of the House of Usher (1839) a visitor reaches a cracked old mansion beside a dark pond, where the last Usher lives with his sickly twin sister. Annabel Lee, the seaside maiden of Poe's last great poem, is often read as his young wife Virginia, dead two years before it appeared. His only finished novel, The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym (1838), sails toward the South Pole, and Jules Verne went on to continue it.

Poe's death is a mystery: found delirious in Baltimore in someone else's clothes, he died in October 1849, said to have called out a name, Reynolds, that no one has traced. In 1996 the cardiologist Michael Benitez blamed rabies.

In 1897 Bram Stoker sent the vampire Count Dracula from Transylvania to England. Arthur Machen, a Welshman, shocked readers in 1894 with The Great God Pan, in which a brain operation lets a young woman glimpse a wild pagan god. Algernon Blackwood's The Willows strands two canoeists on a Danube island among watching bushes, and Lovecraft thought it the best weird tale he knew. Montague Rhodes James, a Cambridge scholar, wrote ghost stories for Christmas, and in Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad a professor digs a bronze whistle out of a Templar ruin and blows it. William Hope Hodgson's The Night Land (1912) shelters the last humans in a vast pyramid on an Earth whose sun has died. The Irish lord Dunsany invented a pantheon in The Gods of Pegana (1905) and wrote his masterpiece, The King of Elfland's Daughter, in 1924; both shaped Lovecraft.

The magazine that gathered the moderns was Weird Tales, first sold in Chicago in March 1923. Its star, Lovecraft, spent almost his whole life in Providence, Rhode Island, apart from a short, unhappy marriage in New York. He died there in 1937 and lies in Swan Point Cemetery, in the family plot, where admirers added a headstone of his own in 1977. His most famous monster, Cthulhu, an octopus-faced giant with dragon wings who sleeps in the sunken city of R'lyeh, first appeared in The Call of Cthulhu in Weird Tales in 1928. In that tale the geometry of R'lyeh is called non-Euclidean, loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours. He also invented a forbidden book, the Necronomicon of the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred. In The Dunwich Horror (1929) the Whateleys of the Massachusetts hills raise a boy, Wilbur, who grows far too fast and goes hunting for that book. Innsmouth is his rotting seaport of staring, fish-faced people and a black reef offshore. In The Whisperer in Darkness (1931) the Vermont hills hide crab-like miners from Yuggoth who carry human brains to the stars in metal cylinders. At the Mountains of Madness, his longest tale, sends a Miskatonic University expedition into Antarctica, where it finds beings who built cities before humanity.

From 1930 Lovecraft wrote long letters to the Texan Robert Howard, arguing civilisation against barbarism, though the two never met. The third star of Weird Tales, Clark Ashton Smith, lived most of his life near Auburn in the California foothills. Smith's stories of Averoigne, an invented province of medieval France, inspired Tom Moldvay's 1981 Dungeons & Dragons module X2, Castle Amber.

When Lovecraft died, his young friends August Derleth and Donald Wandrei set out to save his work. In 1939 they founded Arkham House, named after his invented Massachusetts town, in Sauk City, Wisconsin. Derleth thought his best work was the Sac Prairie Saga, a cycle of books about his corner of Wisconsin. Manly Wade Wellman's guitar-playing Appalachian hero Silver John first appeared in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction in 1951.

howard-burroughs-and-sword-and-sorcery.context_blurb:
Sword and sorcery is fantasy at knife-point: lone fighters, old magic and cities rotten with gold. It grew out of American pulp magazines between the world wars, from Edgar Rice Burroughs's jungle and planet adventures and, above all, from the Texan writer Robert E. Howard.

Burroughs began in 1912 by sending John Carter, a former Confederate cavalryman, to Mars, which its people call Barsoom and where the lighter gravity makes him a superman. Later that year came an English baby orphaned in the African jungle, the heir of Lord and Lady Greystoke, who is raised by a gentle she-ape and grows up as Tarzan. Pellucidar is his hollow Earth, lit by a sun inside it, where dinosaurs still live. Caspak, as its own people call it, is his cliff-ringed island in the South Pacific, where life grows more advanced the farther north one travels. In 1923 he set up his own firm, Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc., to print his books, and the Los Angeles neighborhood of Tarzana is named after his ranch.

Howard, a Texan, created Conan, a black-haired barbarian from cold Cimmeria who roams the Hyborian Age as thief, pirate and mercenary before he seizes the crown of Aquilonia. Howard spent most of his life in the small Texas town of Cross Plains, where his house is now a museum. Conan's first story, The Phoenix on the Sword (1932), is a rewrite of an unsold tale about Howard's earlier king, Kull, called By This Axe I Rule! Kull, an Atlantean, rules the old kingdom of Valusia, and his 1929 story The Shadow Kingdom is often called the first true sword-and-sorcery tale. Before both came Solomon Kane, a grim Puritan swordsman in a slouch hat who arrived in 1928. Bran Mak Morn rules the Picts at the very end of their history, leading his shrinking people against Rome. Beyond the Black River (1935) reads like a frontier Western, and critics say Howard drew its Pictish wilderness from a novel by the American writer Robert Chambers, The Little Red Foot. His only full-length Conan novel, The Hour of the Dragon, was written for a British publisher that went bankrupt, so it first appeared as a Weird Tales serial, and it was later reissued as Conan the Conqueror.

Howard died young, in June 1936, at thirty. From 1950 the small New York firm Gnome Press put Conan between hard covers for the first time. Later writers such as Lin Carter and Sprague de Camp edited and continued the saga.

Fritz Leiber gave the genre its great double act, the towering barbarian Fafhrd and the small, quick thief called the Gray Mouser, first seen in August 1939 in Two Sought Adventure. Their home is Lankhmar, the City of the Black Toga, on the world of Nehwon. The story of how the pair first met, Ill Met in Lankhmar (1970), took both the Nebula and Hugo awards. Leiber also named the genre: in 1961, answering Michael Moorcock in a fanzine, he suggested sword-and-sorcery, and the phrase stuck. Moorcock's own hero, Elric of Melniboné, is an albino sorcerer-emperor whose black sword drinks souls. Karl Edward Wagner, a psychiatrist turned author, created Kane, an immortal swordsman who is the biblical Cain. Older still is Eddison's The Worm Ouroboros (1922), a mock-Elizabethan war epic set, strangely, on the planet Mercury.

Gary Gygax named these writers in Appendix N of the 1979 Dungeon Master's Guide as the reading behind Dungeons & Dragons, alongside one titled nobleman, the Irish fantasist Lord Dunsany.

pulp-heroes-detectives-and-science-ficti.context_blurb:
Between the world wars, cheap magazines printed on rough wood-pulp paper turned masked avengers, tough private eyes and space explorers into heroes for millions of readers. From them grew the hardboiled detective novel and science fiction's golden age, both resting on an older invention, the detective story of Edgar Allan Poe.

Poe created the first modern fictional detective, the Paris thinker Auguste Dupin, in an 1841 tale of two murders in the Rue Morgue. The victims there are Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter, killed in a locked room. Poe called Dupin's method ratiocination, a patient chain of reasoning from small clues. In The Purloined Letter (1844) the police search a minister's rooms in vain for a stolen letter, and Dupin takes up the case. Arthur Conan Doyle owed Sherlock Holmes partly to Poe and partly to his Edinburgh teacher Joseph Bell, who could read a patient's job and travels at a glance.

The pulps' great avenger was the Shadow, a cloaked figure in a slouch hat whose radio broadcasts began with a sinister laugh. In the pulps his true name is Kent Allard, a First World War flier, and Lamont Cranston is only a millionaire whose identity he borrows. Doc Savage, the Man of Bronze, starred in 181 pulp novels with five brilliant helpers. Philip José Farmer's mock biography of 1973 has Doc born aboard a schooner off Andros Island in the Bahamas. Lee Falk's Phantom (1936) wears a purple suit, lives in a Skull Cave in the jungle and seems immortal because each Phantom is the son of the last.

Black Mask magazine built the hardboiled school, and Dashiell Hammett's first star there was the Continental Op, a short, tubby, nameless agent. Hammett's 1930 novel The Maltese Falcon sends Sam Spade after a jewelled bird statue. Raymond Chandler's Los Angeles private eye, Philip Marlowe, first appeared in The Big Sleep (1939). Mickey Spillane's brutal New York detective, Mike Hammer, swore revenge in I, the Jury (1947).

Science fiction had its own editor-king, John Campbell of Astounding. Writing as Don A Stuart, Campbell produced the 1938 novella Who Goes There?, about a shape-shifting alien at an Antarctic station, which John Carpenter filmed as The Thing. Its title is a sentry's challenge, because by the climax nobody can tell who is human and who is the alien wearing a human face. In June 1938 Isaac Asimov, a teenage Columbia student from Brooklyn, brought Campbell a story in person, and in 1939 Astounding printed his Trends. Asimov said that Campbell helped him shape the Three Laws of Robotics, set out in full in Runaround (1942). His first robot story, about a nanny robot named Robbie, was turned down by Campbell and appeared in 1940 under an editor's title, Strange Playfellow. His Foundation series follows Hari Seldon, whose psychohistory predicts the fall of a galactic empire. Robots and Empire (1985) adds a Zeroth Law: a robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm. During the war Robert Heinlein brought Asimov and Sprague de Camp to the Navy Aircraft Materials Center at the Philadelphia shipyard. Heinlein's Starship Troopers (1959) puts Johnny Rico in powered armour against giant bugs. In another Heinlein novel a Martian-raised man teaches the word grok, meaning to understand something so fully that you become part of it.

Frank Herbert's Dune (1965) sends young Paul Atreides to the desert planet Arrakis, home of the sandworms and the spice. Herbert's early outline of the story became Spice Planet, written up by his son Brian and by Kevin Anderson in 2005. Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 (1953) takes its name from the temperature at which book paper burns. Clarke and Kubrick made 2001 together, as novel and film, with its black monolith and the computer HAL 9000. Dick's The Man in the High Castle (1962) imagines a world where the Axis won the Second World War. His 1981 novel VALIS is named for a godlike Vast Active Living Intelligence System. Dick spent his last years filling a huge private journal about his 1974 visions, published in part in 2011 as his Exegesis.

teaches.ac426e5094: His first robot story, about a nanny robot named Robbie, was turned down by Campbell and appeared in 1940 under an editor's title, Strange Playfellow.
teaches.e48f57ec9d: Philip José Farmer's mock biography of 1973 has Doc born aboard a schooner off Andros Island in the Bahamas.
teaches.92eb664b8c: During the war Robert Heinlein brought Asimov and Sprague de Camp to the Navy Aircraft Materials Center at the Philadelphia shipyard.
teaches.f75915f88f: In the pulps his true name is Kent Allard, a First World War flier, and Lamont Cranston is only a millionaire whose identity he borrows.
teaches.17f4d9855c: In The Purloined Letter (1844) the police search a minister's rooms in vain for a stolen letter, and Dupin takes up the case.
teaches.2b67268f96: In June 1938 Isaac Asimov, a teenage Columbia student from Brooklyn, brought Campbell a story in person, and in 1939 Astounding printed his Trends.
teaches.882444c472: Herbert's early outline of the story became Spice Planet, written up by his son Brian and by Kevin Anderson in 2005.
teaches.83d70156bf: His 1981 novel VALIS is named for a godlike Vast Active Living Intelligence System.
teaches.57751b4600: Asimov said that Campbell helped him shape the Three Laws of Robotics, set out in full in Runaround (1942).
teaches.868181d03c: Arthur Conan Doyle owed Sherlock Holmes partly to Poe and partly to his Edinburgh teacher Joseph Bell, who could read a patient's job and travels at a glance.
teaches.0cff034608: Dick spent his last years filling a huge private journal about his 1974 visions, published in part in 2011 as his Exegesis.
teaches.1f25f0ada6: Robots and Empire (1985) adds a Zeroth Law: a robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction allow humanity to come to harm.
teaches.d42fae13d0: In another Heinlein novel a Martian-raised man teaches the word grok, meaning to understand something so fully that you become part of it.
teaches.9b494cdc15: Writing as Don A Stuart, Campbell produced the 1938 novella Who Goes There?, about a shape-shifting alien at an Antarctic station, which John Carpenter filmed as The Thing.
teaches.de905112bd: Poe called Dupin's method ratiocination, a patient chain of reasoning from small clues.
